claims.text: The initial W-Ta-Ti-V-Cr refractory high-entropy alloy has a BCC matrix.
Spark plasma sintering at approximately 1600 °C can consolidate W-Ta-Ti-V-Cr alloys containing in-situ TiC.
Aging at approximately 800 °C after sintering will produce stable, coherent nanoscale TiC precipitates.
In-situ monitoring and iterative heat-treatment adjustment will ensure TiC precipitate stability and coherence.
The intervention will create a uniform dispersion of coherent TiC nanoprecipitates in the BCC matrix.
Coherent TiC-matrix interfaces will act as sinks for irradiation-induced point defects.
Defect capture at the TiC interfaces will enhance vacancy-interstitial recombination.
Enhanced vacancy-interstitial recombination can suppress irradiation-induced void swelling.
The TiC precipitates will reduce radiation-induced defect clustering.
The precipitates will reinforce the matrix through particle hardening.
Coherent precipitate interfaces can facilitate dislocation transmission and reduce stress concentrations or crack initiation.
The TiC-engineered alloy will retain or improve yield strength and ductility relative to the unmodified alloy after irradiation.
The TiC-engineered alloy will accumulate fewer irradiation defects and have a lower void volume fraction than the unmodified baseline.
The modified alloy is targeted to achieve approximately 2.15 GPa strength and 15% ductility under high-temperature irradiation.
The unmodified baseline will develop a higher defect density and may suffer diminished mechanical properties under reactor-relevant irradiation.
The proposed benefit will hold during Ar+, He+, or D+ irradiation at approximately 800 °C and reactor-relevant fluences.
The benefit may diminish if TiC precipitates coarsen or lose coherence at higher temperatures or during extended irradiation.
